clue.text: Where to find a horse firm?

definitions.meaning: the building where a horse is kept overnight

explanation.surface: A riddle asking where you would go to locate a horse, or a company dealing in them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firm' looks like a noun (a business) but it is the adjective meaning steady.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse lives in a stall-lined building of this name, and the adjective also means steady or secure.

clue.text: Unfinished court case covering unusually rare plant pots!

indicators.note: covering means the shortened court case wraps around the other letters
unfinished means the last letter of the word for court case is dropped

parts.note: a court case is a trial

indicators.note: unusually means the letters of rare are rearranged

explanation.surface: An abandoned lawsuit over some rare flowerpots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant pots' is a loose but fair definition: these glass cases hold growing plants.
explanation.definitionFit: Terraria are glass enclosures for growing plants, a fancy kind of pot.

clue.text: Herb one can mostly see in church

parts.note: basil is a culinary herb
the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: mostly means all but the last letter of the word can is used

explanation.surface: Someone spotting basil growing inside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the final N of 'can', leaving CA.
explanation.definitionFit: A basilica is a large church with special privileges granted by the Pope.

clue.text: Venturing to put the compiler up? Mad!

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for the compiler is read from bottom to top

parts.note: the compiler refers to the setter as me
barking (mad) is British slang for crazy

explanation.surface: Someone thinks hoisting the setter is a crazy idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns ME into EM. BARKING is British slang for mad, short for 'barking mad'.
explanation.definitionFit: Embarking on something means setting out on a venture.

clue.text: Battle lines being drawn?

parts.note: read literally: a contest in which two teams pull on a rope, the lines (ropes) being drawn

explanation.definitionFit: This rope-pulling contest is a battle in which a line is literally drawn (pulled) by both sides.

clue.text: What a plastic surgeon does contemptuously?

definitions.text: What a plastic surgeon does contemptuously?

parts.words: What a plastic surgeon does contemptuously?
parts.note: a cosmetic surgeon might literally give a patient a tilted snout; the idiom means to sneer at something

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for showing disdain, read literally, describes reshaping a nose upwards, as cosmetic surgery might.

clue.text: Plan overuse for artist's total output

indicators.note: plan as a verb means arrange, so the letters of overuse are set out anew

explanation.surface: Advice to plan around excessive use when cataloguing a painter's complete works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plan' is the anagram signal on OVERUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Oeuvre is the French-derived term for the whole body of work an artist produces.

clue.text: Where to hold dance in support of factory?

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece supporting another sits beneath it

parts.note: a works is a factory
a hop is an informal dance

explanation.surface: A question about where a factory might host a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in support of' places HOP below WORKS in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A workshop is a room where a session or seminar is held, or where work is held in a vice.

clue.text: Which industry has a tabloid deal?

parts.note: a rag is a disparaging word for a low-quality newspaper
to deal is to trade

explanation.surface: A question about which business a scandal sheet has a contract with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Which industry' is the definition; the answer is a slang name for the clothing business.
explanation.definitionFit: The rag trade is informal British slang for the clothing and fashion business.

clue.text: There's something in a goal that makes the pub angry!

parts.note: cross means annoyed or angry
a bar is a pub

explanation.surface: A football match result so bad that it infuriates the local pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in the clue as pub then angry, but the answer runs CROSS then BAR.
explanation.definitionFit: The horizontal beam joining the two posts is part of a football goal frame.

clue.text: In France you rage about language

parts.note: tu is the familiar French word for you

indicators.note: about means the letters of rage are moved around

explanation.surface: A French speaker being told they are furious about a language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges RAGE into AREG.
explanation.definitionFit: The nomadic Berber people of the Sahara give their name to their Berber tongue, also called Tamasheq.

clue.text: Ducks find a way into the shopping precincts

indicators.note: into means the a and the way go inside the shopping precincts

parts.note: malls are shopping precincts
rd is the abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: Ducks wandering their way into shopping centres.
explanation.walkthrough: 'find' is only a link; RD is the standard abbreviation for road, a way.
explanation.definitionFit: Mallards are the commonest wild ducks, the drake having a green head.

clue.text: It should cancel out mistake about a corner of England

indicators.note: about means the word for mistake goes round the other letters

parts.note: to err is to make a mistake
SE is short for south-east, one corner of England

explanation.surface: A correction meant to remove a blunder about one region of England.
explanation.walkthrough: The English 'corner' is a compass point: the south-east.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubber or eraser removes pencil marks, cancelling out what was written.

clue.text: Nick pastry dishes from the shops!

parts.note: a nick is a chip, a small notch
pies are pastry dishes

explanation.surface: Someone stealing pies from the shops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like the British slang for steal, but it means a chip. Chippies is British slang for fish-and-chip shops.
explanation.definitionFit: Chippies is British slang for takeaways selling fried fish and chips.

clue.text: Leaves regimes at loggerheads!

indicators.note: at loggerheads means in conflict, so the letters of regimes at are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: People departing because governments are quarrelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at loggerheads' shuffles REGIMES AT; the AT is part of the fodder, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To emigrate is to depart one's country to live abroad.

clue.text: People who blossom? Middle class!

parts.note: may is the blossom of the hawthorn tree

indicators.note: middle means the central letter of the word class is taken

explanation.surface: A question about flowering folk, answered with a social rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle class' looks like a social stratum, but 'Middle' picks the centre letter A of 'class'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maya are an indigenous people of Central America and southern Mexico.

clue.text: Methane, hydrogen and oxygen for example found under the planet

indicators.note: in a down clue, pieces found under another sit below it

parts.note: Mars is a planet
H is the chemical symbol for hydrogen
oxygen is an example of a gas

explanation.surface: Chemicals discovered beneath the surface of a planet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found under' puts H + GAS below MARS in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Methane bubbles up from rotting vegetation in wetlands, hence its common name.

clue.text: Itching to be making money after the fourth of July

indicators.note: after means the earning piece comes after the July letter
the fourth of points to letter four of July, not the American holiday

parts.note: earning is making money

explanation.surface: Someone eager to profit once Independence Day has passed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the fourth of July' looks like the US holiday; it is the fourth letter Y of 'July'.
explanation.definitionFit: Yearning means longing, and itching to do something is a strong desire for it.

clue.text: Primates finally moving back for recess

indicators.note: finally moving back means the final letter of the primates word shifts one place back

parts.note: apes are primates

explanation.surface: Apes eventually retreating into an alcove.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letter S of APES moves back a place to give APSE.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is a semicircular recess at the end of a church.

clue.text: Attacked when on top of what the navigator did!

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece on top of another sits above it

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
a navigator sailed a ship

explanation.surface: A naval tale of being assaulted while on deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when' for AS is the conjunction sense, as in 'as the ship left'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be assailed is to be assaulted, violently or with criticism.

clue.text: Morse set out for for Cornwall, and stopped here

definitions.text: Morse set out for for Cornwall, and stopped here

indicators.note: out means the letters of Morse set are put out of their order

explanation.surface: Inspector Morse heading for Cornwall but halting before he gets there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges MORSE SET. The whole clue defines a county one passes through en route to Cornwall from the east; the doubled 'for' is as held.
explanation.definitionFit: This English county lies on the road west towards Cornwall, so a traveller could stop there.

clue.text: Principal actors?

parts.note: looks like leading actors, but means bodies that act on behalf of a principal, as an agent does

explanation.definitionFit: Agencies are organisations acting for clients, who in law are called principals.

clue.text: Bill to demand approval

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill
to claim is to demand

explanation.surface: Asking for praise by presenting an invoice.
explanation.walkthrough: AC is the abbreviation for account, which can mean a bill.
explanation.definitionFit: Acclaim is enthusiastic public praise.

clue.text: Hit by a second lorry!

parts.note: lorry is the British word for truck

explanation.surface: A news line about someone run down by another lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit' is the past participle struck, matching 'Hit by...'.
explanation.definitionFit: Struck is the past form of strike, meaning hit.

clue.text: Shouted — scared me stupid!

indicators.note: stupid suggests muddled thinking, so the letters of scared me are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone yelling that they were frightened senseless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stupid' rearranges SCARED ME.
explanation.definitionFit: To scream is to cry out loudly, a form of shouting.

clue.text: Classical Spanish steel instrument?

parts.note: looks like one instrument made of Spanish steel; really three kinds of one stringed instrument: classical, Spanish and steel-strung

explanation.definitionFit: Classical, Spanish and steel are all named varieties of this six-stringed instrument.

clue.text: Not in form, but better!

parts.note: out is the opposite of in
a form is a school class

explanation.surface: A sportsperson out of form who still wins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form' means a school class, as in British schools.
explanation.definitionFit: To outclass someone is to be far superior, to better them.

clue.text: Indian chief's long story preceding Rome's destruction

indicators.note: preceding means the long story comes before the Rome piece

parts.note: a saga is a long story

indicators.note: destruction means the letters of Rome are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A Native American leader recounting an epic about the sack of Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destruction' rearranges ROME into MORE; the 's of 'chief's' means is.
explanation.definitionFit: A sagamore was a chief among Algonquian peoples of North America.

clue.text: Calm for outwardly simple appointment

indicators.note: outwardly means only the outside letters of simple are used

parts.note: a date is an appointment

explanation.surface: Staying composed for an uncomplicated meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outwardly' takes the first and last letters of 'simple', S and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedate means quiet and unhurried, composed.
